description

Students will learn the applications of mechanics through the examination of mechatronic elements and systems. It covers fundamentals of Mechanics of Materials and Dynamics, including kinematics and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies.

This course will introduce students to the design of complex mechanical systems through the perspective of the mechatronics engineer. Students will learn about forms of power transfer and machine elements such as gears, belts, and lead screws.

This course develops student skills to analyze and design DC and AC circuits. DC topics include resistance, OhmÕs Law, current and voltage division, simplification of circuits, KirchhoffÕs Laws, and nodal analysis.

This laboratory develops skills and practice in the construction, measurement, and analysis of DC and introductory AC circuits. Standard laboratory equipment is introduced and utilized to measure resistance, voltage, and current in basic and relatively complex circuit configurations.

This course covers the analysis, design and implementation of active electronic circuits using diodes, bipolar and field effect transistors and operational amplifiers. The electrical and switching characteristics of semiconductor devices used for analog and digital circuits will be emphasized.

Develops the knowledge of control system concepts and applies them to electromechanical systems. Systems are characterized and modeled using linear systems methods focused with a controls perspective.

This class explores the commonly used engineering metals. Differentiation of materials is made based on an understanding and control of fundamental material properties which informs analysis of which metals are selected for various applications.

This lab class accompanies MCET-110 Foundations of Materials. Emphasis is placed on determining metal properties through experimentation and references, and analyzing why a particular material was selected for an application.

column2: Applications of Fluid Power & Heat Transfer
column10: This course focuses on fluid power, fluid mechanics, flow mechanisms, heat transfer, and the ideal gas laws in the context of mechatronic and robotic systems. Students learn to design and construct pneumatic and hydraulic circuits and controls.
One semester of experience in a job related to the student's major. Department permission is required to add or drop the course.

Common Capstone Project course where students address open-ended problems with emphasis on teamwork, the design process, and project management tools. Cross-disciplinary student teams develop a proposed mechanism or machine identifying customer needs.

This course will provide a thorough understanding of the manufacturing automation principles, practices and system integration. Students will design a fully automated control system specifying the Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) and developing ladder logic.

This course will provide a thorough hands-on experience in using Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) for manufacturing automation and system integration. It includes industry best practices for programming PLCs and essentials of Human Machine Interface (HMI).

This course focuses on the technology and application of robots and automation in the modern manufacturing environment. It provides an understanding of robotic hardware including configurations, drive mechanisms, sensors, and control systems.

First course in a three-course sequence including study of precalculus, continuity, and differentiability. Topics include limits of functions, the definition of the derivative, and applications like optimization and related-rates problems.

Second course in a three-course sequence including Riemann sums, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and techniques of integration. Applications include calculating areas between curves and volumes using the method of slicing.

column2: Elements of Multivariable Calculus and Differential Equations
column10: This course includes an introduction to differential equations, Laplace transforms, and the calculus of functions of two variables. The emphasis is on the application of these topics to problems in engineering technology.

This course introduces statistical methods of extracting meaning from data and basic inferential statistics. Topics include exploratory data analysis, data visualization, the normal distribution, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing.

An elementary introduction to the topics of regression and analysis of variance. The statistical software package Minitab will be used to reinforce these techniques with a focus on business applications.

An introduction to algebra-based physics focusing on thermodynamics, electricity and magnetism, and elementary topics in modern physics. Topics include laws of thermodynamics, electric fields, DC and AC circuits, and the Bohr model of the atom.

This is the first course in a two-course sequence in computational problem solving of engineering and scientific problems. This course will focus on procedural-based coding solutions and will cover topics like sequence, selection, repetitive, and invocation operations.

column2: Introduction to Digital and Microcontroller Systems
column10: This course introduces students to the underlying building blocks of digital system and microcontroller design. Digital systems topics covered include number systems, truth tables, Boolean algebra, combinational and sequential logic, and finite state machines.

This course is an introduction to the cooperative educational program at RIT, the majors in the department, and RIT resources. Topics include the cooperative education placement process and the ethical expectations of employers for co-op students.

Students will apply engineering problem solving methods used in industry to complete projects involving engineering topics such as mechanics, circuits, robotics, and thermodynamics. Software tools are used to work professionally using both written and oral communication software.

A course that integrates basic engineering techniques. Topics will emphasize the design and communication of components through the use of hand sketching, solid modeling, dimensioning, tolerancing, and current GD&T standards.
This course provides an introduction to the analysis and design of structures and machines. Students learn to calculate unknown forces using the concept of equilibrium and free body diagrams.

This course provides coverage of the financial side of engineering decisions relating to product development and operations. It prepares students for the Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) Examination, Engineering Economics section.

Proficiency with traditional machine shop tools will be demonstrated with an emphasis on safety. Students will demonstrate their abilities to interpret drawings and select the appropriate equipment needed to produce parts.

This course will focus on the understanding and application of manufacturing processes. Topics include material properties and process families such as casting, material removal, deformation, and consolidation.

This course introduces students to current best practices in written and visual technical communication. It includes writing, editing, and revising technical information and principles of ethical technical communication.

An introductory algebra-based physics course focusing on mechanics and waves. Topics include kinematics, Newton's laws, rotational dynamics, work and energy, conservation laws, and simple harmonic motion.
